title: Verbs That Change Meaning in the Past

sections.title: A state or an event?
sections.content: You know *saber* and *conocer* from A1 Unit 24, and *querer* and *poder* from A1 Unit 10. These four verbs usually name a state: you know someone, you want something, you are able to do something. In the *imperfecto* they keep that meaning. In the *indefinido* the action becomes a single event with a clear start or end, so the meaning shifts: the moment the state began, an attempt, a refusal or a success. English often needs a different verb for each.

sections.title: Same verb, two tenses
rows: Conocía a Marta. / Conocí a Marta.
I knew Marta. / I met Marta (for the first time).
Sabía la verdad. / Supe la verdad.
I knew the truth. / I found out the truth.
I wanted to leave. / I tried to leave.
No quería ir. / No quise ir.
I did not want to go. / I refused to go.
I was able to leave. / I managed to leave.

items.spanish: Conocí a Lucía en una fiesta; antes no sabía ni su nombre.
items.english: I met Lucía at a party; before that I did not even know her name.

items.spanish: Supimos que había ganado cuando nos llamó su madre.
items.english: We found out he had won when his mother called us.

items.spanish: La jefa no quiso firmar el contrato.
items.english: The boss refused to sign the contract.

items.spanish: Teníamos poco tiempo, pero pudimos llegar a tiempo.
items.english: We had little time, but we managed to arrive in time.

sections.content: Do not translate by tense alone: ask whether something happened (an event) or whether you describe how things were (a state). In the negative, *no quise* is a refusal, while *no pude* means you tried and did not manage. *No quería* and *no podía* keep the plain state: you did not feel like it, or you were not able to.
